content: GPR32, also referred to as G protein-coupled receptor 32 or the RvD1 receptor, is a human receptor that belongs to the rhodopsin-like subfamily of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). It is a protein with an amino acid sequence that shows similarity to other known receptors but does not have any identified ligands to which it responds, nor does it have a clearly defined function. Specifically, GPR32 shares 39% sequence identity with Formyl peptide receptor 1 (FPR1), which is a receptor for N-formylmethionine-leucyl-phenylalanine and related N-formyl peptide chemotactic factors. Additionally, it shares 35% sequence identity with Formyl peptide receptor 2 (FPR2), which also binds N-formyl peptides but is additionally a receptor for certain lipoxins. Lipoxins are metabolites of arachidonic acid and belong to a class of specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs) that function to resolve or inhibit inflammatory responses. Notably, there are no mouse orthologs of GPR32. The GPR32 protein is classified as a G protein-coupled receptor, although the specific G protein subtypes it activates have not yet been identified. It is expressed in various cell types, including activated CD8+ T cells, CD4+ T cells, Th17 cells, tissue macrophages, small airway epithelial cells, and adipose tissue. When expressed in Chinese hamster ovary cells, GPR32 has been shown to inhibit the cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signaling pathway under both baseline and forskolin-stimulated conditions. This suggests that GPR32 is a member of the orphan GPCR class that exhibits constitutive signaling activity. Several specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs), including RvD1, RvD2, AT-RvD1, RvD3, AT-RvD3, and RvD5, activate their target cells through GPR32. This has led to the designation of GPR32 as the RvD1 receptor. Resolvins (RvDs) are members of the SPM class of polyunsaturated fatty acid metabolites. They are derived from the omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and, along with other SPMs, contribute to the inhibition and resolution of a wide range of inflammatory and inflammation-related responses. They also play a role in the healing of inflammatory lesions in both animals and humans. The metabolism of DHA into RvDs and the subsequent activation of GPR32 by these RvDs are proposed to be one of the mechanisms by which omega-3 fatty acids exert their anti-inflammatory effects. This pathway may also contribute to the mitigation of various inflammation-based and other diseases.
